---
title: "Session 9 — Poisson regression with an offset: ship damage"
author: "Prof. Dae-Jin Lee (daelee@faculty.ie.edu)"
output: html_document
---

`MASS::ships` records damage incidents to cargo ships (McCullagh and Nelder, 1989, Sec. 6.3.2).
Each row is a ship `type` (A–E), a construction `year` (60, 65, 70, 75), a `period` of operation (60 = 1960–74, 75 = 1975–79),
the aggregate months of `service`, and the number of `incidents`.
More service means more chances for an incident, so we model the **rate** with an offset.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

## Data

```{r data}
library(MASS)
# Six cells have no service at all: they carry no information about a rate
sh <- subset(ships, service > 0)
sh$year   <- factor(sh$year)
sh$period <- factor(sh$period)
nrow(sh)
head(sh)
```

## Poisson model for the rate

$\log \mu_i = \log(\text{service}_i) + x_i^\top\beta$, so $\mu_i/\text{service}_i = \exp(x_i^\top\beta)$.

```{r fit}
fit <- glm(incidents ~ type + year + period + offset(log(service)),
           family = poisson, data = sh)
summary(fit)
```

## Rate ratios

```{r rr}
round(exp(cbind(RR = coef(fit), confint(fit))), 3)
```

Ships of type B have an incident rate about 0.58 times that of type A ships of the same construction year and period.

## A prediction by hand

```{r by-hand}
b <- coef(fit)
# Type B, built 1965-69, operating 1975-79, 1000 months of service
eta <- log(1000) + b["(Intercept)"] + b["typeB"] + b["year65"] + b["period75"]
unname(exp(eta))
predict(fit, data.frame(type = "B", year = "65", period = "75", service = 1000),
        type = "response")
```

## The offset is a coefficient fixed at 1

```{r free-offset}
fit_free <- glm(incidents ~ type + year + period + log(service),
                family = poisson, data = sh)
coef(fit_free)["log(service)"]   # estimated freely: close to 1?
```

## A first look at fit

```{r fit-check}
c(deviance = deviance(fit), df = df.residual(fit),
  pearson_X2 = sum(residuals(fit, type = "pearson")^2))
```

Both statistics are a bit large for 25 degrees of freedom. Session 10 shows how to measure and handle this.
